summary: Solid, well-sourced, family-friendly core for a 7-10 sentence beginner story. Xunan Kab (Melipona beecheii) is a small stingless bee native to the Yucatan Peninsula that Maya families have kept in hollow log hives (jobones) near their homes since before the Spanish arrived. The Maya treated it as sacred and linked it to the bee god Ah Muzen Cab; its honey was food, trade good, offering and traditional remedy. Meliponicultura (stingless-bee keeping) shrank sharply in the late 20th century (about 93 percent fewer kept hives in Quintana Roo, 1981-2004) because of deforestation, pesticides, hurricanes, competition from the European/Africanized honey bee and fading transmission of the craft; today families, women's groups and schools in Maní, Yaxcaba, Tzucacab, Ich Ek and elsewhere are reviving it. Safest story spine: a child and a grandparent (or a women's group) care for jobones in the yard, thank the bees with a small offering, gather a little honey, and plant flowers and protect the trees so the bees survive. The bee-god and the 1992 oral legend can be added as light, hedged flavor.
facts: Species and name: Xunan Kab is the Yucatec Maya name of Melipona beecheii, a stingless bee native to the Yucatan Peninsula (range reaches Central America to Costa Rica). Glossed as 'lady bee', 'royal lady bee', 'senora abeja', 'dama de la miel'. (CICY 2020; ECOSUR; Gaceta UNAM; Mongabay; Mexico News Daily; Wikipedia; Slow Food)
Stingless but not defenceless: it has no functional stinger; workers defend the nest by biting and clinging. It is docile and easy to manage. (CICY 2020; Slow Food; Mexico News Daily; Tulum Times)

Looks and nest: a small golden-yellow and brown striped bee. Instead of honeycomb it builds small wax pots for honey and pollen. Colonies are permanent, from hundreds to a few thousand bees. (Wikipedia; Mexico News Daily; ECOSUR; Medina presentation says roughly 400 to over 1,200 workers)

Jobones: the Maya name for the hollow log hives in which colonies are kept; one log holds one colony. Logs came from trees such as ramon (Brosimum alicastrum), pich (Enterolobium cyclocarpum) and tzalam (Lysiloma latisiliquum). Families traditionally set them in or around the home garden/yard. (CICY 2020; ECOSUR; Medina presentation; Slow Food; Mexico News Daily)

Hive lids: in 2024 INAH archaeologists announced three round limestone jobon lids (20-25 cm, locally called 'panuchos') found on the Maya Train route in southern Quintana Roo (Bacalar / Felipe Carrillo Puerto area), dated to the Postclassic period (about A.D. 950-1539) and identified as part of an ancient meliponary. Similar lids are still used to plug jobones today. (Mexico News Daily, May 2024)

Ancient roots: keeping this bee goes back to pre-Columbian times; commonly stated as 'at least 3,000 years' (a round estimate, not a measured date). The Postclassic Yucatan was a major hub of honey and wax trade; honey and wax were also demanded as tribute under colonial rule. (Mongabay; Mexico News Daily; Environment & Society Portal; CICY 2020)
Sacred bee: the Maya regarded the bee as sacred, a link between the spiritual and earthly worlds, and honey as a gift from the gods. (Yucatan Today; ECOSUR; Mexico News Daily; Wikipedia)

Ah Muzen Cab is the Maya god of bees and honey, described as guardian/protector of these stingless bees. He is usually shown upside-down (the 'Descending God') at Tulum, Coba and Tankah, holding honey pots/honeycomb and wearing hive-shaped earrings in some descriptions. (Wikipedia; Slow Food; CICY 2020; Mexico News Daily; Tulum Times)

Madrid Codex: this Maya book (Postclassic) devotes several pages to bees, honey and their keeping; the bee in it is generally taken to be Melipona beecheii. (ECOSUR; Medina presentation; Tulum Times; Mexico News Daily - page counts differ, see variants)

Honey uses before and after the conquest: sweetener (the only sweetener the Maya knew), trade and tribute item, ingredient in ceremonial drinks (balche, saka), and traditional medicine. Wax went into candles and moulds. (Slow Food; CICY 2020; ECOSUR)
Honey character: more liquid, more moist and more acidic than ordinary honey, slow to crystallise; amber, creamy, intense and slightly sour taste. (Slow Food; ECOSUR - women's group testimony)

Traditional medicinal use (reported by Maya keepers and ethnographers, NOT clinically proven): eye troubles (cataracts, conjunctivitis), wounds and skin sores, sore throat and respiratory complaints including asthma, digestive upsets, and a food for mothers who have just given birth. Historical colonial-era sources mention headaches, burns, constipation and sore gums. (ECOSUR; Slow Food; CICY 2020; Mongabay; Gaceta UNAM)

Low yield: a Melipona hive gives only about 1 to 2 litres of honey a year, far less than a European honey bee (Apis) hive, which is why the honey is rare and costly. (Mexico News Daily ~2 L; Yucatan Today up to 1.5 L; Tulum Times ~1.5 L; Mongabay about ten times less than Apis)

Harvest practice: keepers take only part of the stored honey, typically around twice a year, leaving the colony enough to survive; over-harvesting can kill a colony. Colonies are multiplied by dividing a strong hive (traditionally near the full moon in one account). (Tulum Times; ScienceDaily/STRI; Mongabay)

Bee ceremonies: 'U Jaanli Kab' (also spelled U Hanli Kab), 'the meal/food of the bees', is a thanksgiving offering to the bees and their protector deities, linked to the honey harvest; 'U Jeets Luumil Kab' asks for good weather and blooming for the next honey season. A maize drink (saka) is offered. (CICY 2020; Tulum Times; Maní meliponary description via search)

Women and school revival: women's groups such as Koolel Kab (Ich Ek, Campeche, since 1995; 'women who work with bees'), Melitz'aak (Felipe Carrillo Puerto, Quintana Roo), Las Vecinas (Tzucacab, Yucatan) and women trained in Yaxcaba are rescuing jobones and selling honey and honey products; the school U Yits Ka'an in Mani teaches stingless-bee keeping. (ECOSUR; Mongabay; Mexico News Daily; Por Esto/WWF via search)

Villages and keepers named in sources: Yaxcaba (Don Josue Ake Pech, jobon he estimates over 200 years old), Mani (U Yits Ka'an school, Kuxtail cooperative), Tzucacab (Las Vecinas), Xaya (Flor de Jazmin meliponary, 95 hives) and Chacsinkin (keeper Antonia Ku Yah), Ich Ek (Campeche). A 2020 CICY list of Yucatan municipalities with keepers includes Abala, Chumayel, Dzan, Hocaba, Mani, Oxkutzcab, Sacalum, Tekax, Valladolid and Yaxcaba. (Mexico News Daily; EcoAmericas; CICY 2020; ECOSUR; Mongabay)

Decline numbers: Villanueva-G, Roubik and Colli-Ucan (Bee World 86(2), 2005) reported more than 1,000 kept hives in the 1980s, about 400 in 1990 and about 90 in 2004 among Quintana Roo keepers, commonly summarised as a 93 percent fall in about 25 years. Most remaining keepers were older men. (ScienceDaily/STRI 2005; Mongabay; EcoAmericas; Wikipedia)

Why the bee and the craft are endangered (consistent across sources): forest loss and fragmentation (farming, cattle, towns, citrus), hurricanes and drought/heat, pesticides and agrochemicals, competition and substitution by the European/Africanized honey bee (Apis mellifera, more productive), over-harvesting and poaching of wild nests, and loss of traditional knowledge because young people leave and elders stop keeping bees. (CICY 2020; ScienceDaily/STRI; Mongabay; Slow Food; Por Esto; Environment & Society Portal)
Wild nests are now rare because they need hollows in large old trees; the bee also forages high in the canopy. (Environment & Society Portal; Villanueva-G et al.)
Ecological role: the bee is an important native pollinator of wild forest plants and of crops such as habanero chili and tomato. (CICY 2020; Slow Food; Gaceta UNAM)

Old tie between maize farming and bees: traditional shifting milpa cultivation fitted well with stingless beekeeping; de Jong (Utrecht thesis 1999) argues the craft became less sustainable after the conquest as farming changed. (Utrecht University portal)

Oral legend (one recorded version): told by dona Teresa Conrado de Ucan in Merida, March 1992, transcribed by Sergio Medellin Morales, printed in a 1993 UNAM veterinary thesis on meliponiculture. A bee god brings a honeycomb in his hands to a princess and tells her to place it in a log she herself prepares and to raise the bees; the honey will be a banquet for princes and kings. She must not turn to look at the god, so he leaves and is never seen again. She multiplies the hives and shares them with her servants so they can keep bees too. 'That is how we have the xunan kab, queen of all bees.' (UNAM thesis TES01000192718)
variants: Name gloss: 'lady bee' / 'royal lady bee' (Wikipedia, Tulum Times, Gaceta UNAM) vs 'senora abeja' (Mongabay) vs 'dama de la miel / lady of honey' (ECOSUR, Slow Food). Core: xunan = lady, kab = bee/honey.

Alternative bee names: Kolel Kab ('dama de la miel') and Pool Kab are given in CICY 2020 and the Medina presentation as other Maya names for the same bee; Spanish Wikipedia says the Yucatec Maya called this species kolel-kab and that xunan kab is used loosely for stingless bees in general. Core: Xunan Kab is the best-known, safest name.
Spelling of the bee: Xunan Kab / Xunaan Kab / Xunan-Kab / Xunaan Kaab / Xuna'an Kab. Spelling of the hive: jobon / jobón (plural jobones) / hobon.
Spelling of the god: Ah Muzen Cab, Ah Musen Kab, Ah Mucen Cab/Kab, Ah Muzencab, Muzencab, Ah Muzankab, Ah Muu Zen Caab. Core: use 'Ah Muzen Cab'.
Madrid Codex bee pages: 10 pages (Medina presentation, Tulum Times), 14 pages (Mexico News Daily), page 108 (Environment & Society Portal). Core: 'several pages'.

Honey per hive per year: about 1.5 L (Yucatan Today, Tulum Times), about 2 L (Mexico News Daily), 3-5 L (one other press report seen only in a search summary), up to 1 L falling to 0.3 L in drought (EcoAmericas). Core: 'one to two litres at most'.
Number of stingless-bee species on the peninsula: 16 (Mongabay, Slow Food, Mexico News Daily) vs 13 still surviving (Explore Yucatan 2020). Core: 'about sixteen species, Xunan Kab is the best known'.

Decline numbers refer to kept hives of Quintana Roo keepers (Villanueva-G 2005); some media wrongly generalise to 'the whole peninsula' or 'the species'. Press also repeated the authors' projection that the craft could vanish by 2008; it did not, and revival projects have grown since.

Ceremony names and timing: U Jaanli Kab (CICY, Mani sources) vs U Hanli Kab (Tulum Times, Universidad Veracruzana snippet); second ritual U Jeets Luumil Kab vs 'u hedz luumil cab' (Tulum Times says it is performed when hives are moved or added; CICY says it asks for ideal honey-making conditions). Timing: October festival (Mongabay), June and December near full moon (Tulum Times). Core: a thanksgiving ceremony for the bees tied to the honey harvest.

Identity of the 'Descending God': INAH and Ralph Roys read it as bee god Ah Muzen Cab; some specialists read it as Venus or a setting-sun/transition symbol; Wikipedia hedges ('may be the same figure'). Core: tell it as 'many people connect the diving figure at Tulum to the bee god'.
Role of Ah Muzen Cab: 'guardian of the bees' (CICY, Slow Food) vs creator/underworld figure in Chilam Balam and 'great red bee' (Wikipedia, ECOSUR). Core: protector of the bees and honey.
Colony size: hundreds to over a thousand workers (Medina) vs 'dozens to thousands' (CICY). Core: 'a small colony'.

Honey property claims: antibacterial/antiviral/anti-inflammatory (Mexico News Daily, no citation), antioxidant and antibacterial lab studies exist (CICY, Chimal 2023 per search summary). Core: 'traditionally used as medicine'.

maya_terms.meaning: 'lady bee' / 'royal lady bee' / 'lady of the honey'; the stingless bee Melipona beecheii. Pronounce roughly shoo-NAHN kahb.
'lady of honey'; another Yucatec name for the same bee. As Koolel Kab also the name of a women's beekeeping group in Ich Ek, Campeche ('women who work with bees').
third name given for Melipona beecheii in CICY 2020; meaning not glossed in the sources.
bee and honey (also earth/land in Maya generally). Appears in all the bee names.
hollow log used as a hive for one colony of stingless bees.
'bee house'; a house or shelter for the hives (Medina presentation).

maya_terms.term: Ah Muzen Cab (Ah Mucen Kab, Ah Musen Kab)
maya_terms.meaning: Maya god of bees and honey, protector of the bees; shown upside-down.
'Great Lord of the Hives'; a bee deity name given by one source (Yucatan Today) only.
'the meal/food of the bees'; thanksgiving offering ceremony for the bees.
ceremony asking for good weather, flowers and conditions for honey (spelling and exact purpose vary).
ritual maize drink offered to bees/gods.
ritual fermented drink made with the bark of the balche tree and honey; alcoholic, central to Maya ceremonies and banned in colonial times.
another stingless bee (Trigona/Frieseomelitta nigra); one of the other native stingless bees.
Maya name of another Melipona, Melipona yucatanica (Medina presentation).
names of two other stingless bees (Trigona fulviventris; Plebeia species).
'dew of the sky'; agroecological school in Mani that teaches stingless-bee keeping.
Maya women's beekeeping cooperative in Felipe Carrillo Puerto, Quintana Roo.
Spanish terms: keeping stingless bees / the keeper / the place with the hives (from tribe Meliponini).
Spanish commercial/colloquial label for raw, unprocessed melipona honey; no official definition found (see cautions).
the traditional maize field (Spanish word of Nahuatl origin); closely tied to the bees in village life.
village ceremonies 'bring the rain' and 'meal of the milpa' (ECOSUR); related agricultural rituals, not bee-specific.

sources: Villanueva-G, R., Roubik, D.W. and Colli-Ucan, W. 2005. Extinction of Melipona beecheii and traditional beekeeping in the Yucatan Peninsula. Bee World 86(2): 35-41 (read via ScienceDaily/STRI summary and secondary reports)
cautions: Medical claims: honey as medicine is traditional/ethnographic and mostly not clinically validated. The story must not tell children to put honey in eyes, treat illness or replace a doctor; keep it to 'grandma says it is good for a sore throat' at most, or avoid health claims entirely.

Religion: Ah Muzen Cab and the ceremonies are real Maya religious practice. Present gently and in the past tense or as 'some families still thank the bees', not as instruction or as the narrator's belief; avoid describing rituals as magic, sacrifice or idolatry. Do not mention colonial-era persecution details in a beginner story.

Balche is an alcoholic ceremonial drink and the 'sacrifice of animals' appears in ECOSUR's account of old farm rituals: leave both out. If an offering is mentioned use food, flowers, a little honey or a candle only.
Descending God identification is contested (bee god vs Venus). Hedge with 'many people think' or skip the Tulum link; do not state it as fact.

The 1992 legend is a single recorded version told in Merida, not a pan-Maya canonical myth, and it stresses the princess being 'virgen'. Either omit the virginity framing or paraphrase as 'a kind, honest girl'; credit as 'a story told in Yucatan'. Do not present it as ancient scripture.

'Miel virgen' has no official definition; the only usage found (a 2005 Universidad Veracruzana note, https://www.uv.mx/universo-hemeroteca/177/central/central.htm, seen via search snippet only) uses 'virgen' as a market label for melipona honey. Safer in the story: 'miel pura' or simply 'la miel de Xunan Kab', or gloss 'miel virgen' as honey taken straight from the hive without heating or mixing.

'Endangered': scientists and press say the bee and the craft are in serious decline, but I found no IUCN Red List assessment (Spanish Wikipedia lists it as not evaluated) and could not confirm NOM-059 status. Say 'in danger of disappearing' or 'becoming rare', not 'officially endangered'. Avoid the keeper's quote that it could vanish 'in five years' (an opinion, not a projection).

Numbers vary by source and year (hives per colony, litres per hive, prices per litre, number of species, producers). Use none or only round, hedged ones ('one or two litres a year', 'many fewer hives than before').

Several sources are journalism, tourism or promotional pages (Tulum Times, mayan.org, Yucatan Today, Por Esto). Their specifics (4-6 ceremonies a year, 500 ancient hives, 'unbroken cult', Hobnil festival in month Tzec, Noh Yum Kab) are single-source and were left out of the core facts or flagged. The strongest sources are CICY, ECOSUR, Villanueva-G et al. 2005, de Jong 1999, UNAM and INAH reporting.
Ceremony names (U Jaanli/Hanli Kab, U Jeets/Hedz Luumil Kab) have unstable spelling across sources; use one spelling consistently and keep the gloss 'meal of the bees'.
The bees do bite when disturbed even without a sting: do not write that they are completely harmless or encourage children to open hives; a keeper (adult) opens the jobon.

Do not claim the Maya 'invented' beekeeping or that Xunan Kab is the only honey bee the Maya kept (they also kept other stingless species such as Trigona, though M. beecheii was the favourite and the main producer).

Recent items I saw only in search summaries and did not verify (Mexico Supreme Court considering legal rights for melipona bees; Quintana Roo denomination of origin for melipona honey; Por Esto 2025-26 articles): keep out of the story.

Language-teaching note: Maya words (Xunan Kab, jobon, kab) are best presented as a few glossed loanwords inside Spanish sentences; avoid full Maya grammar since orthography is not standardised across the sources.
